item.title: Watch: Gangsters battle family and rivals in high-octane ‘Mirzapur The Movie’ trailer
item.description: The screen version of the Prime Video series adds Ravi Kishan and Jitendra Kumar to the cast.
item.content:encoded:
The popular Prime Video series Mirzapur has yielded a screen adaptation. The Hindi film brings back the show’s favourite characters alongside new faces. Characters who perished are back on the screen (except Vikrant Massey).

Directed by Gurmmeet Singh (who also helmed the web series), Mirzapur The Movie sees Akhandanand (Pankaj Tripathi) locked in a power struggle with his wayward son Munna (Duvyenndu), his wife Beena (Rasika Dugal) and his challenger Guddu (Ali Fazal).

Ravi Kishan is among the additions to the film, playing Akhandanand’s rival. Jitendra Kumar plays Guddu’s confidante.

Also in the film are Shweta Tripathi as Golu, Shriya Pilgaonkar as Sweety, Harshita Gaur as Dimpy alongside Kulbhushan Kharbhanda, Sheeba Chadha, Rajesh Tailang, Shubhrajyoti Barat, Sushant Singh and Abhishek Banerjee.

The trailer promises the cocktail of brutal action, small-town swagger and punchline-heavy dialogue that made the series popular. The day you sit on the throne, you forge an unshakeable bond with death, Akhandanand says. Written by Puneet Krishna and scored by John Stewart Eduri, the film is scheduled to be released on September 4 in cinemas.

item.title: Poochmaxxing: The pet wellness sector is booming
item.description: There are some simple things you can do that are supported by science and do not cost a small fortune.
item.content:encoded:
I am a runner who loves being active alongside my dogs. Actually, I am more of a plodder – and one with very bad knees. Those knees benefit from regular physiotherapy and sports massage. You might not be surprised, then, to hear that I have regular physiotherapy appointments. The slight curveball is that the last three appointments I have attended have been with my dogs’ veterinary physiotherapist.

Yes, you read that right. Before sorting out my own physical ailments, I took each of my dogs for a full musculoskeletal assessment where they had an individual exercise plan prepared. They also each benefited from some canine sports massage and laser therapy during their session.

They were then driven home, resting on orthopaedic bedding, while wearing magnetic therapy coats. Once home, they were fed meals specifically prepared for their individual needs, topped with fresh ingredients and supplements intended to support specific aspects of their health.

Meanwhile, I, their chauffeur and chief carer, was drinking instant coffee, nursing aching knees and wearing an ancient hoodie complete with a few “fashionable” holes. At one point, as I stood up creakily, I even joked to their physiotherapist: “Do you do people?” She politely declined.

item.title: Amit Shah is ‘coward’ for not attending Parliament, says Congress
item.description: Union minister Kiren Rijiju said that the government was ready for ‘detailed discussion’, and accused Rahul Gandhi of ‘running away’ and shouting slogans.
item.content:encoded:
The Congress on Tuesday said that Union Home Minister Amit Shah was a “coward” for not being present in the Lok Sabha as the Opposition continued to demand a discussion on police action against youth protesters in Delhi on July 20.

Congress leader Jairam Ramesh said Shah was a “no-show” in the Lok Sabha despite business being listed against his name. He said that Shah’s absence from both Houses for 17 sitting days was “truly unprecedented”.

“Once again, he has proved that those who intimidate are themselves cowards,” Ramesh said.

The Monsoon Session, which began on July 20, is scheduled to conclude on Thursday.

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju rejected the charge, saying that the government was ready for a “complete and detailed discussion” on the students’ protests and police action and that Shah was ready with his reply. He accused Congress leader Rahul Gandhi of having “run away” and shouting slogans outside Parliament instead of participating in the debate, ANI reported.

item.title: Roads in India are a deadly risk to the world’s smallest wild cat
item.description: The rusty-spotted cat is prone to being killed by vehicles due its small size, among other factors, say researchers.
item.content:encoded:
Scientists at the Wildlife Institute of India have reported two roadkill incidents of the rusty-spotted cat (Prionailurus rubiginosus) at the National Chambal Sanctuary in Etawah, Uttar Pradesh. The two records are the first documented occurrence of the small carnivore in southern Uttar Pradesh, according to the research paper published in the Journal of Threatened Taxa in May.

Roadkill data for small carnivores is heavily underreported, and these records were “a matter of chance”, according to Vishnupriya Kolipakam, a Wildlife Institute of India scientist and one of the paper’s authors.

While they add a new locality to the small cat’s known range, the wildlife sanctuary falls within its distribution range, Kolipakam said. “The wild cat has been reported from areas all around Chambal, including Kuno, Rangarh-Vishdhar, Ranthambhore, and Dholpur,” she said.

However, this follows a pattern, as seen in recent papers that have curated sighting reports of the strictly nocturnal cat. There were nine records of roadkill from the Saurashtra Peninsula in Gujarat between 2016 and 2024, and four records from Rajasthan between 2000 and 2020. In Nepal, too, where the cat was discovered as recently as 2016, there has been a record of a roadkill.

For an elusive small cat that has been rarely observed in the wild, these roadkill records add up to a significant number....

item.title: Dhruv Rathee video on Hindu deities withheld in India after Centre’s order, Google tells Delhi HC
item.description: The petitioner submitted that the video was accessible in India via VPN and sought its global removal, alleging that it hurt the sentiments of Sanatan Dharma.
item.content:encoded:
A video by YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in which he claimed that Hindu gods consumed meat was blocked in India following a Union government order, Live Law quoted Google as informing the Delhi High Court on Tuesday.

The video remains accessible outside India, while a request for its global removal is pending before a division bench of the High Court, Google’s counsel told Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma.

The plea seeking removal of the video was filed by lawyer Amita Sachdeva. Rathee had uploaded it on YouTube on March 21, In it, he discussed dietary habits in Hindu scriptures. He noted that texts have mentioned that deities like Ram and Krishna consumed meat and alcohol.

Sachdeva alleged that the video was derogatory, inflammatory and communally sensitive. She also filed a criminal complaint against Rathee before a magistrate, alleging that he had distorted Hindu scriptures and “mocked the sanctity of Sanatan Dharma”.

Sanatana Dharma is a term some people use as a synonym for Hinduism.

The Union government’s Grievance Appellate Committee had ordered the video to be blocked after the High Court on July 3 asked the Centre to decide on the plea, Bar and Bench reported.

The Grievance Appellate Committee hears appeals by users against social media intermediaries regarding complaints about online content.

item.title: Bill criminalising insults to ‘Vande Mataram’ becomes law after President Murmu’s assent
item.description: Intentionally preventing the singing of the song or disrupting an assembly singing it can be punished with imprisonment of up to three years, the law states.
item.content:encoded:
President Droupadi Murmu on Thursday gave assent to a bill criminalising insults to the national song, Vande Mataram.

With the president’s assent, the 2026 Prevention of Insults to National Honour Amendment Bill has become law.

The Lok Sabha passed the legislation on July 30 through a voice vote amid protests by Opposition MPs demanding a discussion on police action against youth protesters on July 20. The Rajya Sabha cleared it a day earlier.

The protests on July 20 were held against alleged mismanagement in the conduct of competitive examinations.

The law gives Vande Mataram the same statutory protection as the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana. It states that intentionally preventing the singing of the national song, or disrupting an assembly singing it can be punished with imprisonment of up to three years, a fine or both.

The 1971 Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act already makes insulting the national anthem, national flag or Constitution punishable with up to three years’ imprisonment, a fine, or both.

The legislation had faced opposition from the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam in the Lok Sabha, with MP Kanimozhi accusing the government of advancing a “Hindutva agenda” under the cover of nationalism.

Responding to the debate, Minister of State for Home Affairs Nityanand Rai said the legislation was about “Indian pride” and was not directed against any state or ideology.

item.title: Tamil Nadu Assembly passes resolution seeking abolition of NEET
item.description: The move came amid an ongoing anti-NEET hunger strike in Chennai, which entered its 11th day on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
The Tamil Nadu Assembly on Tuesday unanimously adopted a resolution urging the Union government to abolish the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for undergraduate medical admissions and allow the state to admit students based on their Class 12 marks, The Hindu reported.

NEET is currently mandatory for admission to undergraduate medical courses in India.

The lone Bharatiya Janata Party MLA, M Bhojarajan, opposed the resolution and walked out before the vote.

Moving the resolution, Health Minister KG Arunraj urged the Union government to amend the 2019 National Medical Commission Act, the 2020 National Commission for Indian System of Medicine Act and the 2020 National Commission for Homoeopathy Act to enable admissions based on Class 12 results.

The resolution said that Tamil Nadu had consistently opposed NEET on grounds of social justice, equality and the rights of states in a federal system. It also said repeated question-paper leaks and other irregularities had further undermined confidence in the examination.

It also referred to the cancellation of the 2026 undergraduate medical admission exam and the subsequent re-examination, saying the developments had caused “untold mental agony” to lakhs of students and resulted in the loss of young lives.

“The examination has forfeited the trust of the students of this country,” The Hindu quoted the resolution as saying.

Abhirup Paul was arrested for allegedly shouting slogans in support of jailed activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam.

Paul and another fellow student of the institute were also booked for possessing downloaded books and other material that the prosecution alleged reflected Maoist ideology.

item.title: Bengal SIR: SC says it cannot set timeline for tribunals hearing appeals against voter deletions
item.description: The Supreme Court, however, sought details from the Election Commission on pending and disposed cases before the appellate tribunals.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday said it cannot set a timeline for appellate tribunals hearing challenges to deletions from electoral rolls in West Bengal during the special intensive revision, Live Law reported.

However, the court asked the Election Commission to provide details of cases disposed of and pending before the tribunals.

A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant was hearing a petition filed by Congress leader Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury seeking speedy disposal of cases related to the voter roll revision exercise.

On July 8, the Calcutta High Court verbally observed that pending appeals against voter deletions under the special intensive revision process would take “21 years…if appellate tribunals function at the current pace”.

The special intensive revision of voter rolls in West Bengal was carried out before the Assembly elections in April.

Final rolls published in February initially excluded more than 61 lakh voters, with the process continuing through supplementary lists and adjudication of about 60 lakh “doubtful and pending” cases.

By April 6, about 91 lakh voters, nearly 11.9% of West Bengal’s electorate before the revision process began, had been removed from the electoral rolls.

item.title: Using history and the present, a new book argues that Enlightenment ideals are not universal
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Chromatic World Order: The Fiction That Rules Our World: A Brief History of its Genesis and Other Stories’, by Sajid Mohamed.
item.content:encoded:
When one considers the contradictions between the Enlightenment’s stated ideals and their practical implementation, for example, if we take the case of the American Revolution, which was one of the earliest implementations of the movement inspired by Enlightenment principles such as liberty, equality, and natural rights, and note that it coexisted with chattel slavery, we find that the Enlightenment ideals functioned as an ideological framework that could also coexist with, without any disturbance in its coexistence with a profoundly unequal and racialised society. Enslaved individuals could be, without needing an extraordinary example or explanation, constitutionally counted as three-fifths of a person for purposes of representation.

The US Constitution is an early, large-scale application of Enlightenment ideals that, at the same time, reveals the racially restricted claim to universality. Solomon Northup’s Twelve Years a Slave is a well-noted critique of the inconsistency of American democracy, particularly the coexistence of constitutional freedom and institutionalised slavery.

Northup, born a free Black man, who was enslaved and then later freed through legal intervention, appealed to reason and human dignity, and challenged, early on, the point being made here – that in the superficial universality of Enlightenment ideals within a racial order, Black or, by extension, coloured lives were expendable....

item.title: Centre introduces bill in Lok Sabha to restrict states from imposing taxes on mineral rights
item.description: The bill, introduced by Union minister G Kishan Reddy on Monday, also seeks to empower the Union government to regulate mineral-bearing lands.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government on Monday introduced a bill in the Lok Sabha to restrict states from imposing additional tax on mineral rights, PTI reported.

The bill also seeks to empower the Union government to regulate mineral-bearing lands in accordance with the parameters prescribed under the 1957 Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation Act, the news agency reported.

Union Minister of Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy introduced the 2026 Mines and Minerals Development and Regulation Amendment Bill amid protests by Opposition members.

According to the bill, “no tax, cess or such other levy (by whatever name called) shall be imposed by the state government on mineral rights”.

The proposed provisions would cover mineral-bearing lands, with their applicability determined by factors such as the quantity or value of minerals, royalty payments or other prescribed criteria. Such lands would be subject to conditions and restrictions specified by the Union government, PTI reported.

The bill, however, clarifies that any tax, cess or other levy on mineral rights or mineral-bearing lands that was paid to or collected by a state government before the provisions take effect “shall not be liable to be refunded”.

Reddy said that the amendments seek to “provide certainty, stability and predictability in the fiscal regime in the mineral sector,” the news agency reported.

item.title: Allahabad HC orders Rs 25 lakh compensation to sisters confined by father for converting to Islam
item.description: Depriving them of their liberty was ‘an exceptionally grave and egregious violation of constitutional rights’, held the court.
item.content:encoded:
The Allahabad High Court has ordered the Uttar Pradesh government and the father of two women, who voluntarily converted to Islam, to pay them Rs 25 lakh in compensation for unlawfully confining them.

In a judgement delivered on August 6, Justice Sandeep Jain also ordered that the sisters be released. ,

Jain held that they were liable to get compensation for the “unlawful deprivation” of their fundamental rights. Their confinement amounted to “an exceptionally grave and egregious violation of constitutional rights”, he added.

The two sisters, aged 20 and 35, had told the court that they had voluntarily converted from Hinduism to Islam and decided to marry as per their own wishes, which was their fundamental right. They denied having changed their faith because of force, fraud or “undue influence”.

The sisters alleged that their father had confined them inside their paternal home after they converted.

In his judgement, Jain said that he interacted independently with both women and found that their responses were “spontaneous, coherent and unequivocal”. The judge held that the sisters, as adults, had the legal capacity to take decisions about their lives.

item.title: 132 killed as 7.4-magnitude earthquake hits Colombia
item.description: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in only three days ago, has declared a state of emergency.
item.content:encoded:
At least 132 persons were killed after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia on Monday, stated the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, a non-profit organisation. Additionally, 483 persons were injured.

The toll is likely to rise as several persons are feared trapped under collapsed buildings, reported the BBC.

The earthquake struck at 7.34 am local time and damaged at least 1,500 buildings, reported AFP. The epicentre was near the village of San José del Palmar, in Chocó province.

The cities of Cali, Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales were most affected by the quake. It was also felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama.

This was the strongest earthquake recorded in Colombia in the 21st century and it was followed by several aftershocks, AP quoted the country’s Geological Service as saying.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in only three days ago, has declared a state of emergency.

“We aren’t going to leave people alone,” he was quoted as saying by the AP. “They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination.”

Hospitals in five Colombian cities were put on red alert Monday. A nighttime curfew has been declared in Cali.

Six airports have suspended operations, according to AFP.

item.title: The ‘left-behind’ India: Global trade deals can have disruptive political consequences
item.description: The economic benefits are concentrated in a few places, deepening regional inequality and prompting migration which fuels nativist backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Amid talk of fractures in world trade, India continues to pursue globalisation as an economic development strategy. After a decade without any trade deals, India signed agreements with the European Union, United Kingdom, and New Zealand over 2025 and 2026, and is continuing negotiations with the US and other regions, signaling a renewed commitment to global economic integration. Most analyses of these agreements emphasise their geopolitical implications, especially for India’s emerging-power status and strategic relationship with the US, China, and Russia.

But these new deals will also contribute to the transformation of India’s domestic political economy. From India’s initial liberalisation in 1991, to its (re)emergence as a major exporter of textiles and apparel, to its dominant position in information technology services, globalisation has reshaped economic opportunity, social conflict, and political outcomes.

This transformation has touched areas intensely integrated with the global economy, but also localities that are little exposed to world markets. These new agreements, which grant extensive access to lucrative export markets, will likely catalyse deeper connections between India and the global economy.

item.title: A new book examines sculptor Meera Mukherjee’s legacy to look closely at artistic labour
item.description: An excerpt from ‘From the Depth of the Mould: Meera Mukherjee (1923-1998), A Centenary Tribute’, edited by Tapati Guha-Thakurta.
item.content:encoded:
A gigantic female figure opens a window high above her head to look out into the sky. Her face is turned away from viewers as her massive arms pull up the shutters. When this work by Meera Mukherjee was first exhibited in the galleries of the Birla Academy of Art and Culture, Kolkata, in 1993, it carried the title Akash [Sky]. The centre-piece of that exhibition, it towered towards the ceiling of the room, appearing to push itself out into the open. Like her other larger-than-life figures, this sculpture also seemed to demand its place under the open skies, although its permanent home would become the gallery of another Birla art museum in Hyderabad. Bulldozers and construction crews are reshaping parts of Nairobi’s best-known informal settlement, Kibera. In a video shared by President William Ruto, new apartment blocks rise alongside existing corrugated-iron structures, while new roads cut through the settlement. The message is clear: Kenya’s affordable housing programme is bringing modern housing to one of the country’s most visible symbols of urban poverty.

The redevelopment forms part of Ruto’s broader affordable housing programme, which aims to deliver 200,000 housing units annually, combining social housing, affordable homes and market-rate units. By March 2026, government figures indicated that 8,367 units had been completed since Ruto took office in September 2022, with many more at various stages of construction across the country. Completed units therefore remain well below the programme’s stated annual target.

Supporters see it as a long-overdue investment in urban infrastructure and housing. Critics, however, have challenged the compulsory levy used to finance the programme: employees pay 1.5% of their gross monthly salary, matched by a 1.5% employer contribution, while people outside formal employment pay 1.5% of their gross income. They have also raised concerns about whether the homes will be affordable to lower-income households and allocated transparently.

item.title: Should India apologise for caste injustice, like Nepal did?
item.description: A formal apology may not lead to concrete changes. Instead, pursuing reparations could help reimagine the project of social justice in India.
item.content:encoded:
“Why should I have to pay for something my ancestors did?” That is a refrain frequently heard from members of the upper castes during discussions about casteist violence and prejudice or reservations in India.

This belief has found renewed expression in the “Reservation Hatao Movement”, a social media campaign that gained visibility in late July. It calls for the abolition of caste-based reservation so that “merit” and equal competition can prevail.

Many Indians believe that caste is a relic of a bygone time and that the government’s social justice policies have addressed these problems.

This ignores the inherited control over land, wealth, education, social networks and institutions through which caste privilege reproduces itself, presenting outcomes produced by historical inequality as though they emerged from neutral competition among equals.

The Indian state, similarly, speaks the language of social justice without unsettling the structures of social power that shape Indian society.

It is against the backdrop of this refusal of historical accountability that Nepal’s decision to offer a formal state apology to Dalits for centuries of caste-based oppression acquired significance in India. item.title: How to make the most of boredom
item.description: Boredom may be good for us if we effectively tap into its full potential.
item.content:encoded:
Boredom is something many of us will do everything we can to avoid. We fill our time with social media, books and TV programmes and keeping our schedules packed with plans.

But boredom doesn’t always need to be seen as something negative. Boredom may, in fact, be good for you – but only if you effectively tap into its full potential.

1. It can push you towards positive change

Boredom tends to arise when we want to be mentally engaged but our current activity or environment isn’t providing the level of challenge, stimulation or meaning we need. This can leave us feeling restless – especially if we don’t know how to remedy the situation.

It’s for this reason that boredom can be used to push ourselves towards change and encourage exploration.

But in order to make boredom really work for you, it’s vital to avoid just reaching for the next easy distraction, like scrolling on your phone, online shopping or visiting the pantry for a snack.

Positive change comes not from asking “how do I stop feeling like this?” but asking yourself “what meaningful thing do I need next?” Focusing on doing something meaningful is key to making boredom a bridge to more productive or positive activities.

item.title: On India’s western coastline, ‘ghost’ fishing gear is causing marine pollution
item.description: Damaged nets and their pieces slip into the Arabian Sea where they continue trapping fish, turtles and other marine life.
item.content:encoded:
In the early light at Thoppumpady fishing harbour in the city of Kochi, coils of blue and green nylon nets lay heaped on the concrete docks, stiff with salt after a long night at sea. Many had been patched and repatched so often that they were barely holding together. Nets too damaged to mend are often cut loose offshore. Once they sink, few are ever recovered.

Across India’s west coast, lost fishing gear known as “ghost gear” has become a significant source of marine pollution. Nets vanish whole or in fragments, slipping into the waters of the Arabian Sea where they continue trapping fish, turtles and other marine life long after fishers abandon them.

India operates one of the world’s largest marine fishing sectors, supporting an estimated 14.5 million livelihoods along more than 7,500 kilometres of coastline.

While national estimates are scarce, a 2022 study in the southwestern state of Kerala, where Kochi is located, found that fishers lost, abandoned or discarded about 21% of their fishing gear annually. That’s more than 10 times the global average of 1.82% estimated by another study, which highlights the scale of material entering India’s marine environment.

The clarification came two days after the Lok Sabha passed the Taxation and Other Laws Amendment Bill 2026, which would allow banks and other service providers to levy charges on payments through UPI and RuPay debit cards.

Sharing its name with the coast of its origin, the language of Konkani is spoken in multiple dialects and written in scripts as diverse as Perso-Arabic, Roman, Devanagari, Kannada, and Malayalam. Enmeshed within the politics of language, so closely tied to regional identity in South Asia, official status, standardisation, and patronage pertaining to the scripts and languages in which Goan literary production occurs have been matters of long-standing concern in the enclave.

Located on the Konkan coast, Goa’s linguistic and literary heritage outsizes the region’s diminutive geography. Konkani is one of the languages in which Goan writers have expressed their craft in Romi and Nagri scripts, but Goan literature also appears in Marathi, English, and Portuguese. item.title: In photos: How festivals and rituals help Koraput’s Adivasis keep local seed varieties alive
item.description: On World Indigenous Peoples Day, a glimpse at how agricultural biodiversity is woven into everyday life, preserving local knowledge over generations.
item.content:encoded:
The first pot of rice newly harvested during October-November is never eaten straight away in Koraput. Before families gather around the meal, a portion is offered to the village deity. Around five to six months later, the next farming season begins with prayers for rain, while wooden ploughs, cattle and seeds are honoured in their own ceremonies.

In Koraput, in the Eastern Ghats of southern Odisha, every stage of cultivation has its own festival. The region is home to the Paroja, Gadaba, Kondh, Bhumia, Bhottada, Durua and Saura Adivasi communities. Here, agriculture is intrinsically linked with culinary heritage and faith.

Koraput is among India’s richest centres of crop diversity. It harbours hundreds of locally adapted crop varieties, including indigenous paddy, finger millet, little millet, pigeon pea, black gram, horse gram, niger, sesame, traditional vegetables, tubers and wild edible plants.

Unlike monoculture farming, fields here are planted with a diverse mix of crops that support one another, reduce farming risks and provide food throughout the year. Farmers cultivate varieties of rice that mature at different times, ensuring that all crops do not ripen at once. This helps spread the risk when rainfall is delayed or uneven.

item.title: ‘Iran’s Grand Strategy’: A nuanced understanding of how historical trauma is embedded in statecraft

Vali Nasr’s Iran’s Grand Strategy: A Political History is one of the most vital works that demand attention during the ongoing Iran-America standoff. The author argues that Iran’s strategy is not driven by ideology alone, but shaped by a collective memory of invasions, humiliation, foreign interference, and a deep-seated fear of national disintegration. To understand the politics of the Islamic regime, one has to understand the historical psychology behind it.

According to Nasr, the Islamic Republic views itself as both isolated and vulnerable because the Arab Sunni states surround it, while it possesses a distinct Persian identity fused with Shi’ism. Under the Safavids, especially Shah Ismail I, Shi’ism became Iran’s state religion as a strategic decision helping distinguish Iran from its Sunni Ottoman and Uzbek rivals. The United States is reviewing a proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period that allows certain foreign workers on non-immigrant visas to remain in the country and look for a new job after losing employment.

If finalised, foreign workers covered under the rule and their dependents would have to leave the US immediately if their employment ends before their authorised stay expires. They would be unable to change status or change employers within the country, unless US Citizenship and Immigration Services its discretion to forgive the lapse in status.

The 60-day grace period was introduced in 2017. It applies to several categories of temporary employment visas, including H-1B visas for workers in special occupations, L-1 visas for employees transferred within multinational companies, O-1 visas for persons with extraordinary ability.

The Department of Homeland Security has the discretion to shorten or refuse the grace period, although it has rarely done so, PTI reported.

The proposal from the Department of Homeland Security is currently under review by the federal Office of Management and Budget.

The details of the proposed regulation were not immediately known.

Over the past few years, Indians have constituted the majority of H-1B visa holders. Indians comprised 72.3% of all H-1B visas issued by the US in the financial year 2022-’23.

item.title: Does ‘training to failure’ build better muscle strength?
item.description: Stopping shortly before failure can preserve technique and reduce fatigue while providing an effective training stimulus.
item.content:encoded:
It is easy to assume that harder training always produces better results. In resistance training, which includes lifting weights or using resistance machines, taking every set to the point where you cannot complete another repetition may create more fatigue without producing better results.

A repetition, or rep, is one complete movement of an exercise. A set is a group of repetitions performed without a long rest.

Training to failure means continuing a set until you cannot complete another full repetition with acceptable technique, despite making your best effort. This is sometimes called momentary muscular failure.

An alternative is to stop while you could still perform one or more repetitions. This is described as repetitions in reserve, or RIR. If you could complete 10 repetitions but stop after eight, you have two repetitions in reserve, usually written as 2 RIR.

Why might training close to failure help?

Muscles are made up of individual cells called muscle fibres. These fibres are broadly classified as type 1 or type 2 fibres and are controlled by the nervous system. The type 2 fibres produce more force and can grow more than type 1 fibres.

item.title: Homer’s ‘Odyssey’: Who is Nausicaa, the bold princess who helped Odysseus go home?
item.description: It’s a shame Nausicaa was left out of Nolan’s ‘Odyssey’: she is a good example of how Homer’s Odyssey is ‘a woman’s poem’, as many scholars have recognised.
item.content:encoded:
In Homer’s Odyssey, Nausicaa is a tall, gutsy teenage princess who finds a naked and helpless Odysseus washed up on her shore, gives him her brothers’ clothing, and instructs him on how to appeal to her mother, Queen Arete, for help to get home to Ithaca. She is crucial to his eventual return home after 20 years’ absence.

But she doesn’t appear in Christopher Nolan’s film at all – and her absence is part of a broader debate about how his version reduces or simplifies the role of women in the epic poem. In the Guardian, classicist Emily Hauser mourned the absence of the “delightfully brash princess”, along with nuance and complexity.

“There are more female characters than in most Nolan movies, thanks to the source material,” wrote classics professor Emily Wilson, whose translation of The Odyssey is a critically acclaimed bestseller, this week. “But none of them has much to say, in contrast to the characterisations in the poem.”

This applies to several key characters, from the enchantress Circe, who turned Odysseus’ men into pigs, to Odysseus’ wife Penelope. But what about the absent Nausicaa? Who was she? And why was she important?

On that August day in 1941, the monsoon skies had opened up, yet thousands of people turned up to pay their last respects to Bengal’s greatest creative artist and humanist. Then, the crowd swelled into a mob, and the final procession turned into a grotesque affair. There were stories of a virtual stampede, and people – no one was sure who they were – wild with grief started pulling at the poet’s hair. I have spent the last five years reading climate fiction for my PhD research – which sounds more glamorous than it is. It means a lot of late nights with dystopian novels, many scribbled margins, and a slowly accumulating awareness that most adult climate fiction, for all its ambition, tends to land in one of two traps: it either drowns the reader in despair, or it resolves the crisis a little too neatly. What it rarely does is leave you with something as simple as hope that feels earned. Which is why Rajat Chaudhuri’s Wonder Tales for a Warming Planet surprised me.

I came to this lucid and compact illustrated collection shortly after submitting my thesis, in that odd, untethered week when you don’t quite know what to do with yourself. There was a time when writers would escape to the hills, spending their days with trees, streams, and wildlife, seeking inspiration for their art. This romantic notion of the hills is amply felt in literary works born from such circumstances, which in turn, compel the reader to believe that the mountains are sites of pristine beauty and undisturbed peace. Writings across genres – poetry, travelogue, fiction – unanimously agree that there are few things as majestic as a mountain. Gurgaon over many centuries was little more than a small rural hamlet in the periphery of the towering city of power Delhi. Across the ages possibly its best known resident was Hemu Vikramaditya, a general in the army of Sher Shah Suri who defeated the forces of Humayun and later Akbar. Gurgaon gained some modest standing only as the customary resting place for Akbar’s entourage when they marched to Amber.

Its fortunes altered after Independence. Badly singed by the fires of the Partition riots in 1947-’48, Gurgaon was substantially emptied of its Muslim population. When Carla Montemayor discovers that her great-great-grandmother was a binukot – a girl sequestered from her family and community, trained to memorise and sing the myths of her people – this sets her on her own epic journey to uncover her ancestry. Why was she raised on European fairytales and Greek myths when the stories of her own people are so rich? And why did no one in her family speak of their illustrious binukot foremother anymore?

Travelling to the Philippines to trace the lives of her female relatives, Montemayor discovers that, officially, her people have no history. Like many indigenous groups, their stories have been erased by colonists. It becomes her work to reconstruct and reimagine them.

Weaving together the tales of her family members, who survived war, oppression, violence, displacement and more, with the myths of her people, Montemayor finds similarities: women with courage, resourcefulness and ambition, who fight and love with equal ferocity.

Mudassir Ramzan’s novella The Man from Kashmir opens with an epigraph from James Joyce’s Ulysses: “History…is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake.”

These lines are spoken by Stephen Dedalus in an uncomfortable conversation with his headmaster, Mr Deasy. Deasy rambles on about his own narrow views – British nationalism, religion, and a grand divine purpose moving history toward a predetermined goal. Stephen counters this view by perceiving history as chaotic, relentless, filled with violence and trauma.

Ramzan’s novella may well be read as the history and becoming of young Dedalus. Ahmed – born in a mosque of the fictional town, Poshmarg, and raised within a particular Kashmiri Muslim texture – dies at the end by suicide in a foreign land. In his prehistory and disintegration are the lives and stories of his tribe that finally weigh him down. When Ahmed’s friend Peter asks Rahil about his profession, he replies:

“What does any brown man with a degree in the humanities do in academia? Colonial studies. Postcolonial literature of India and Africa. He had also been working on a book about Kashmir – specifically, the application of postcolonial theory to the region.”

item.title: Indian court rulings on the ‘right to be forgotten’ will dent our collective memory
item.description: A string of judgements have weaponised the fundamental right to privacy against journalism, databases and search engines.
item.content:encoded:
They say that the first draft of history is written by journalists. This is mostly true, except perhaps in the case of legal history where the first draft is written in the records of the courts by its stenographers and judges. It is these records which capture the present and preserve it for posterity in public and private archives for historians of the future.

As the world moved into the digital age, the information technology revolution promised to make it easier than ever to store, index and organise records. The information revolution also converted much of the internet into an archive which was meticulously indexed by search engines for the common citizen to use for free. So much so that the first draft of history today depends upon the first page of search results displayed by Google’s algorithm.

All of this is at risk today because of a string of judgements tumbling out of the High Courts across India which have weaponised the fundamental right to privacy against journalism, databases and search engines. item.title: Is it worse to eat junk food early in the day?
item.description: The body can process food more efficiently in the morning but blood sugar spikes and hunger pangs can quickly crop up after an unhealthy meal.
item.content:encoded:
Many of us have grown up with the mantra that breakfast is the most important meal of the day.

But whether it’s snatching an extra half hour of sleep, or focusing on getting the kids out of the house, there are various reasons why assembling a healthy breakfast might slip down your list of priorities – especially on a weekday.

So, is it worse to eat unhealthy foods first thing, compared to later in the day? And what about skipping breakfast altogether?

It’s not just about calories

You probably know eating foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fats – especially when they’re highly processed – puts you at greater risk of a range of serious health conditions. These include diabetes, heart disease and some cancers.

Poor diet can also affect our gut health, mental health and reproductive health.

Eating a diet high in vegetables and fruit, lean meat and alternatives, such as chicken and lentils, wholegrains, and reduced-fat dairy and alternatives (such as plant-based yoghurt) will improve your overall health and wellbeing, and reduce the risk of serious health conditions.

For breakfast, aim to include a source of good-quality protein, wholegrains, fruit and/or vegetables and healthy fats.

item.title: UP: Muslim driver dies four days after being assaulted by kanwariyas following road accident
item.description: A purported video of the incident has been shared widely on social media which shows Azeem Ali being attacked by a group in the presence of a police officer.
item.content:encoded:
A 24-year-old Muslim truck driver died of his injuries four days after he was assaulted by a group of kanwariyas in Hapur district in Uttar Pradesh, The Print reported on Friday.

The assault followed an argument after Azeem Ali’s truck collided with an auto-rickshaw hired by the kanwariyas in Garhmukhteshwar town on July 31. The collision allegedly injured the auto-rickshaw driver, Farman, who was standing near the vehicle. Ali was then allegedly pulled out of his truck and assaulted.

A purported video of the incident has been shared widely on social media which shows Ali being assaulted by a group of men in the presence of a police officer.

Ali was initially taken to hospital in Meerut and later shifted to Delhi as his condition worsened. He reportedly went into a coma and died at a Delhi hospital on Tuesday, The Print reported.

A first information report has been registered against seven persons, including four kanwariyas, in connection with Ali’s murder.

Five persons identified as Manish, Ankit, Lokesh, Shivam and Farman, along with two unidentified persons, have been booked under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita pertaining to murder, rioting and voluntarily causing hurt, The Print reported.

item.title: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye sign defence pact amid conflict in West Asia
item.description: India said that it was ‘closely following’ the agreement.
item.content:encoded:
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on Friday signed a joint defence agreement on Friday, amid the conflict in West Asia.

India said that it was “closely following” the new defence pact.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, is aimed at “strengthening collective deterrence” and states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be considered an attack against all.

It also seeks to enhance defence cooperation among the three countries and promote peace, security and stability in the region and beyond.

However, the agreement does not specify detailed military commitments or obligations that have been accepted, Reuters reported.

An unidentified Turkish official told the news agency that the pact was “purely defensive in nature” and was not directed against any particular country.

The official added that the pact was open to other regional countries and would not replace existing bilateral or multilateral defence arrangements.

The agreement was signed by Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

It came against the backdrop of heightened tensions in West Asia amid conflict involving Iran, Israel and the United States.

The pact brings together three major Sunni Muslim-majority states: Saudi Arabia, the Gulf’s strongest economy, one of the world’s top oil exporters and home to Islam’s holiest sites, Pakistan, the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority country and Türkiye, which has North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s second-largest military.

item.title: Nepal’s demolition drive leaves thousands homeless, violates human rights
item.description: The government and armed forces evicted mostly poor and marginalised residents of Kathmandu.
item.content:encoded:
The mass eviction of slums and informal settlements in Nepal’s capital Kathmandu and surrounding districts has displaced an estimated 15,000-20,000 people.

On April 25, the Nepal government began forcibly removing landless residents from the Kathmandu Valley, later extending the drive beyond the capital.

Nepal faces a staggering crisis: more than 3.5 million people are landless or homeless. A government commission invited applications for registration, and 1.2 million people – mostly poor, Dalit, and indigenous – have already registered in the hope of receiving land. Ironically, these communities have borne the brunt of evictions carried out without adequate notice, consultation, or alternative housing. The lack of support has eroded their trust in the state.

The ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party pledged to resolve landlessness within 1,000 days of office. Its 100-point action plan also promised relief to the landless. Yet, despite decades of settlement – some families have been living in Kathmandu’s slums for 60 years – the government demolished homes using the full force of the state. Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, Nepal Army, and the municipal police participated. Residents were harassed, threatened, and even detained before demolitions.

item.description: How did a drug meant to treat diabetes become India’s top-selling drug within months of its launch?
item.content:encoded:
We went undercover to investigate the booming market for Mounjaro, an injectable that apart from type-II diabetes, can also be prescribed by specialist doctors for severe and complicated obesity. Effective for weight loss, it is not meant for everyone and should not be used without medical advice.

But, as we found, the prescription-only drug is available on tap. From chemist shops and online sellers agreeing to sell Mounjaro without a prescription to unauthorised doctors prescribing the drug as part of beauty treatments in aesthetic salons, many are profiting from India’s obsession with weight-loss – at a steep cost to the health of users.

item.title: FCRA amendments India’s internal matter: Centre after US lawmaker calls bill ‘attack’ on Christians
item.description: Congressman Riley Moore had warned that the proposed changes to the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act could hurt bilateral relations.
item.content:encoded:
The Ministry of External Affairs on Friday said that proposed amendments to the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act were India’s “internal affairs”, three days after a United States Congressman raised concerns about the move.

Registration under the Act is mandatory for non-profit organisations to receive foreign funds. A key provision of the draft legislation allows the Union government to take control of a non-governmental organisation’s foreign funds and assets if its FCRA registration lapses or is cancelled.

On Tuesday, Riley Moore, a Republican representative from West Virginia, criticised the proposed amendments, claiming that the Indian Parliament was trying to take control of churches and religious charities.

“Christians have been in India since St Thomas the Apostle travelled to the Malabar Coast just decades after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Moore said on social media.

Despite this long history, India’s Parliament is considering amending the rules “to permit government takeovers of churches and religious charities”, he alleged.

He said that the bill would be “a clear attack against Christians” and claimed the move could hurt relations between Washington and New Delhi.

The bill was introduced in Parliament in March during the Budget Session but has not been cleared by either of the Houses.

item.title: Jharkhand protests: Ink thrown at student leader Neha Bora allegedly for supporting Umar Khalid
item.description: The All India Students’ Association president alleged that the man shouted ‘Jai Shri Ram’ after the incident.
item.content:encoded:
Ink was thrown at student leader Neha Bora on Friday during a protest in Ranchi against alleged irregularities in recruitment exams in Jharkhand. The police have detained the alleged attacker, PTI reported.

The man, who was detained by the police, said that he had targeted Bora because of her support for jailed activist Umar Khalid, PTI reported.

“I do not like Neha Bora because she supports Umar Khalid,” PTI quoted him as saying. “…They are all anti-nationals.”

Khalid has been in jail since September 2020 for his alleged involvement in the communal violence that broke out in North East Delhi in February 2020 between supporters of the contentious Citizenship Amendment Act and those opposing it. The violence had left 53 dead and hundreds injured. Most of those killed were Muslims.

Bora is the president of the All India Students’ Association, the student wing of the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist).

item.title: Bengal: Two BJP workers named in CBI chargesheet for murder of CM Suvendu Adhikari’s aide
item.description: One of them arranged and financed the killing by hiring shooters from Uttar Pradesh, alleged the investigation agency.
item.content:encoded:
Two Bharatiya Janata Party workers were among the 11 persons named in a chargesheet filed by the Central Bureau of Investigation in connection with the murder of an aide to West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, PTI quoted unidentified officials as saying on Thursday.

Chandranath Rath was shot dead near Kolkata on May 6, two days after the West Bengal Assembly election results were declared. Adhikari, who became the chief minister on May 9, was not with Rath at the time of the attack. The BJP leader has alleged that it was a “pre-planned murder”.

Since taking over the investigation into Rath’s murder on May 12, the CBI has arrested 11 persons.

The two BJP workers named by the investigation agency are brothers Sagar Sonkar and Sahib Sonkar, The Hindu reported. They were arrested on August 1.

Sagar Sonkar had worked with Rath and was one of the key conspirators in his murder, an unidentified official was quoted as claiming by the newspaper. He allegedly arranged and financed the killing by hiring shooters from Uttar Pradesh.

He worked for an MLA from a rival political party until 2020, before joining the BJP, PTI quoted the CBI as claiming.

item.title: Audio clip allegedly linking Manipur violence to former CM is manipulated, Centre tells SC
item.description: The government urged the bench to dismiss the plea that demanded an independent investigation into the recording.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government on Friday claimed before the Supreme Court that the audio clip allegedly linking former Manipur Chief Minister N Biren Singh to the ethnic violence in the state was manipulated, Bar and Bench reported.

The court was hearing a petition filed by the Kuki Organization for Human Rights Trust, which has demanded an independent investigation into the audio clips purportedly featuring Singh’s voice.

The government’s submission came after the National Forensic Sciences University in Gujarat’s Gandhinagar placed on record a forensics report about the authenticity of the clip.

Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, representing the Union government, quoted an expert at the separate Central Forensic Science Laboratories as having stated that the full audio clip had 41 alterations, Bar and Bench reported.

The counsel urged the bench of Justices Sanjay Kumar and Sanjeev Sachdeva to dismiss the petition.

However, the bench ordered that a copy of the National Forensic Sciences University’s report be provided to the petitioner and the government, saying that both sides will be given an opportunity to address its content, the legal news outlet reported.

item.title: Nashik TCS case: AIMIM corporator arrested for ignoring court summonses
item.description: Matin Patel has been named in the chargesheet for allegedly providing refuge to Nida Khan, the main accused person in the sexual harassment matter.
item.content:encoded:
The Maharashtra Police has arrested All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen corporator Matin Patel for not responding to summonses issued by a court in connection with a sexual harassment case at the Tata Consultancy Services in Nashik, The Indian Express reported.

Patel was held after the court issued a non-bailable warrant against him for skipping two summonses.

The corporator has been named in the chargesheet for allegedly providing refuge to Nida Khan, the main accused in the case, despite knowing that her anticipatory bail plea had been rejected.

While the police were searching for Khan in April and May, “it was revealed through confidential information and technical analysis” that Patel had provided her shelter to help her evade arrest, The Indian Express cited the chargesheet as having alleged.

Khan was arrested on May 7 from a bungalow in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar’s Naregaon area that was owned by Patel.

She was held more than 40 days after being named in a first information report for allegedly hurting religious sentiments.

item.title: ‘DC’ review: ‘Devdas’ gets a violent reimagining but fires blanks
item.description: Arun Matheswaran’s Tamil action thriller stars Lokesh Kanagaraj in his acting debut alongside Wamiqa Gabbi.
item.content:encoded:
Having made his share of action thrillers, Lokesh Kanagaraj now stars in one. Arun Matheswaran’s DC stars the curly-haired director as the ‘D’ in ‘DC’: Devadas.

Yup, the same one who ruined himself through obsessive love and alcohol in Sarat Chandra Chatterjee’s classic novel Devdas. In DC, made in Tamil and dubbed into Telugu and Hindi, the destruction is turned outward while the alcohol continues to be copiously imbibed.

If ashes could turn, they would.

Kanagaraj’s Devadas is the leading light of a gang of armed robbers. Their latest heist brings them in the crosshairs of the police officer Bhojraj (Krish Dayal), who is keenly following the advice given to him by his boss: “Be brutal.”

Devadas and his mates, including Kitty (Avinash Raghudevan), go on the run, cutting down whoever crosses their path. But a heart of gold throbs behind Devadas’s epilated chest, compelling him to behave like Robin Hood when required and fall for sad-faced women who are awaiting rescue.

Devadas doesn’t succeed with the club singer Parvathi (Sanjana AK) but fares better with the rose-clutching sex worker Chandra (Wamiqa Gabbi).
